lines: When Splatoon 2 made its ink too shiny, the splashes of an enemy diving in became harder to see. How did the ink lighting need to be adjusted?
The starting point was the first game’s ink. Some areas looked overly shiny or too flat. For the sequel, physically based shading was adopted to model how light and materials interact.
But dark shading on the raised ink made the boundary between your team’s color and the opposing color harder to distinguish.
They then removed the shading. The colors were easier to distinguish, but it became harder to read which parts of the three-dimensional terrain were walls and which were floors.
They also strengthened specular reflection: the bright sheen created by reflected light. Then the splashes made by an enemy turning into a squid and diving into ink became harder to see.

Three things needed to remain readable together: the two ink colors, the shape of the terrain, and the signs of an enemy diving in. The ink’s shading and sheen were adjusted so those signals would not be buried.
